content:
According to Bloomberg, bipartisan US senators are urging Apple CEO Tim Cook to commit by August 21 that the company will not adopt memory chips from Chinese suppliers Changxin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC). The full report is as follows.

Background

Apple is trying to address an ongoing memory chip shortage and has reportedly sought approval from the Trump administration to source components from CXMT and YMTC; both companies have been placed on the Chinese military companies list by the US Department of Defense.

Legally, Apple does not need US government approval to purchase chips from these companies, but if it proceeds without government backing, the company could face significant political consequences.

As a result, Apple CEO Tim Cook, in an interview with The Wall Street Journal shortly before the latest price hike, said "all options should be on the table" and added that "we should consider all sources of supply."

In the days that followed, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple had been seeking government assurances in order to purchase CXMT's chips, while the Financial Times reported that Apple was in talks with YMTC to purchase chips. The Financial Times later further reported that Apple is testing CXMT's DRAM chips.

Earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple's use of Chinese memory chips may not be limited to the Chinese market, and said the company is seeking government approval to use components from CXMT and YMTC in products sold outside the United States.

The report also detailed that Micron is actively lobbying the government to reject Apple's request, on the grounds that allowing Chinese suppliers into Apple's supply chain could undermine domestic US memory production.

This is not the first time Apple has attempted to purchase memory chips from YMTC. In 2022, the company explored using the supplier's components in some iPhones sold in China, but the plan was shelved after it drew the attention of US lawmakers and export controls tightened.

Senator Marco Rubio, who at the time served as vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, condemned Apple for "playing with fire," and lawmakers from both parties warned that the deal could pose a national security risk.

Lawmakers Pile On Pressure

Bloomberg reports today that "a group of bipartisan US senators is urging Apple to abandon any move to purchase chips from blacklisted Chinese semiconductor suppliers (CXMT) and (YMTC), and warning the iPhone maker that it will face the risk of relying on a hostile nation for critical components."

The lawmakers reportedly described Apple's plans as "short-sighted," and said the move would "ensure that the world's most valuable consumer electronics company becomes increasingly dependent on a supplier formally designated by the US government as a Chinese military company for critical components."

The lawmakers also pointed out that other companies could follow Apple's lead, which could harm domestic US memory production, as well as planned investment projects in states such as Indiana, Idaho, New York, and Virginia.

They added that any initial measures to confine CXMT memory chips to products sold in China would be difficult to maintain, because "once a component passes Apple's production qualification, deploying it globally is only a procurement decision away."

Finally, beyond demanding that Apple commit by August 21 to "avoid using memory from CXMT or YMTC in its products," the senators also asked Apple to provide detailed information on any data shared with CXMT during the component qualification process, noting that the transfer of controlled technology data to advanced Chinese chipmaking facilities may require Commerce Department approval.

Apple did not immediately respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.
